messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] negative binomial confusing doc
messages.body_plain:
Hi, they are not the same. Inverse scale was a bad choice of name that I
had.

In fact, the parameter phi of neg_binomial_2 is the same of the
parameter alpha (shape) of neg_binomial. It is also the parameter r of
wikipedia's definition of negative binomial (number of failures until
the experiment is stopped).

But I don't think it should be called shape either, nor use the same
greek letter of neg_binomial (alpha), they reason is that, while they
are the same parameter, their interpretation is very different in the
three parameterizations mentioned above (because the other parameters
are different):

In neg_binomial, when we change alpha, with all other things held
constant, the mean and the variance increase. (the same is true for
wikipedia's r)

In neg_binomial_2, when we change phi, with all other things held
constant, the mean is held constant and the variance decreases.

For this reason, I think the best naming for phi is precision parameter,
or even better phi^-1 is the overdispersion parameter (seems more in
tune with literature).

messages.subject: latexmk?
messages.body_plain:
Anyone have any experience with latexmk?

I'm thinking of using that to build our manual. It'll handle dependencies a lot more generally than whatever dependency rules I can make.

Here's how to run it. From within src/docs/stan-reference/:
> latexmk -pdf -pdflatex="pdflatex -interactive=nonstopmode" -use-make src/docs/stan-reference/stan-reference.tex

It would add an additional dependency on Perl for anyone that wants to build the manual. On Mac and Linux, I don't think that's an issue. On Windows, it's not part of anything we suggest people to install, but this is really a dev-only procedure. Anyone downloading a tarball will have the built pdf.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I think Andrew's proposing estimating the mass matrix this way,
not a posterior somewhere.

There are a gazillion papers out there on low-rank matrix
estimation in the specific context of covariance.   Martin
Wainwright gave a nice departmental seminar a year or two ago
on a mixture sparsity prior of what I recall to be a low-rank
approximation and a heavily L1-regularized approximation.

For some problems, you actually know some of the sparsity structure
in advance, so you can optimize there.

- Bob

messages.subject: cut is multiple imputation (and easy in Stan)
messages.subject_clean: cut is multiple imputation (and easy in Stan)
messages.body_plain:
I read Lunn, Best, Spiegelhalter, et al.'s 2009 paper on cut:

  Combining MCMC with ‘sequential’ PKPD modelling

  http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10928-008-9109-1

The PDF's a bit wonky, but I could read it.

WHY
==========================

They describe their intent for cut as an intermediate between

  * using a point estimate for PK parameters in the
    PD model (aka "sequential" PK/PD), and

  * doing full PK/PD joint inference.

The problem with the sequential approach is that the PK point estimates
don't propagate any uncertainty, whereas the problem with the latter
is that the PD model warps the PK inferences so that they are no longer
realistic (I have to take their word for it --- the warped version didn't look
so unreasonable to me, but them I'm not a pharmacologist!).

Lunn et al. do recognize that the latter problem arises due to misspecification
in the PD model, but apparently nobody knows how to fix the PD models.  In the meantime,
they'd rather cut than let the PK predictions wander outside of reasonable values.

There's a simpler measurement error linear regression in the BUGS
book, where they want to propagate lack of certainty in the measurements,
but not allow the measurement error model to float the latent measurements
back to an almost exact fit with little uncertainty in the regression parameters.
I wasn't convinced looking at that example, either, but it's simpler than PK/PD.

WHAT
==========================

As Lunn et al. point out, cut in BUGS is similar to Rubin and
Little's notion of multiple imputation (which I think matches
Andrew's).  But rather than literally doing multiple imputation
and then fitting a PD model for each PK parameter draw, they
provide performance improvements in the form of the BUGS cut
operation that lets you do the imputation and fitting all in
one system.

Lunn et al. introduce some new graphical model notation for
cut, but it boils down to a function,

   u <- cut(v),

the behavior of which is to assign the value of v to u, but otherwise
cut any information flow from u back to v.

STAN
==========================

To implement cut in Stan, we could copy the value of an autodiff
variable into a new autodiff variable with no partial linked back
to the original variable.  Absolutely trivial to implement, though
harder to doc.

You could even hack it this way in the current version of Stan if
your variables are around unit scale:

  u <- round(1e10 * v) / 1e10;

This may make it easier to explain to at least some people why
functions like round() and floor() are so problematic!

DISCLAIMER
==========================

Now before anyone locks down the GitHub repo to try and stop this
madness, let me just say we have no plan to actually implement cut()
in Stan!

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I don't think that idea for implementing cut() in Stan would actually do anything other than make the sampling less efficient.  In particular, the gradient is used to simulate the Hamiltonian so cutting the flow of gradient information will change the path that is simulated, but the ending state is accepted or rejected based on a Metropolis test which is what ensures that the chain maintains the proper invariant distribution.  Changing the Hamiltonian (by changing the gradient) will not change the invariant distribution in any way, it will just make it more likely that the Metropolis test rejects the sample.

Cheers,
Marcus

>> I read Lunn, Best, Spiegelhalter, et al.'s 2009 paper on cut:
>>
>>  Combining MCMC with 'sequential' PKPD modelling
>>
>>  http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10928-008-9109-1
>>
>> The PDF's a bit wonky, but I could read it.
>>
>>
>> WHY
>> ==========================
>>
>> They describe their intent for cut as an intermediate between
>>
>>  * using a point estimate for PK parameters in the
>>    PD model (aka "sequential" PK/PD), and
>>
>>  * doing full PK/PD joint inference.
>>
>> The problem with the sequential approach is that the PK point estimates
>> don't propagate any uncertainty, whereas the problem with the latter
>> is that the PD model warps the PK inferences so that they are no longer
>> realistic (I have to take their word for it --- the warped version didn't look
>> so unreasonable to me, but them I'm not a pharmacologist!).
>>
>> Lunn et al. do recognize that the latter problem arises due to misspecification
>> in the PD model, but apparently nobody knows how to fix the PD models.  In the meantime,
>> they'd rather cut than let the PK predictions wander outside of reasonable values.
>>
>> There's a simpler measurement error linear regression in the BUGS
>> book, where they want to propagate lack of certainty in the measurements,
>> but not allow the measurement error model to float the latent measurements
>> back to an almost exact fit with little uncertainty in the regression parameters.
>> I wasn't convinced looking at that example, either, but it's simpler than PK/PD.
>>
>>
>> WHAT
>> ==========================
>>
>> As Lunn et al. point out, cut in BUGS is similar to Rubin and
>> Little's notion of multiple imputation (which I think matches
>> Andrew's).  But rather than literally doing multiple imputation
>> and then fitting a PD model for each PK parameter draw, they
>> provide performance improvements in the form of the BUGS cut
>> operation that lets you do the imputation and fitting all in
>> one system.
>>
>> Lunn et al. introduce some new graphical model notation for
>> cut, but it boils down to a function,
>>
>>   u <- cut(v),
>>
>> the behavior of which is to assign the value of v to u, but otherwise
>> cut any information flow from u back to v.
>>
>>
>> STAN
>> ==========================
>>
>> To implement cut in Stan, we could copy the value of an autodiff
>> variable into a new autodiff variable with no partial linked back
>> to the original variable.  Absolutely trivial to implement, though
>> harder to doc.
>>
>> You could even hack it this way in the current version of Stan if
>> your variables are around unit scale:
>>
>>  u <- round(1e10 * v) / 1e10;
>>
>> This may make it easier to explain to at least some people why
>> functions like round() and floor() are so problematic!
>>
>>
>> DISCLAIMER
>> ==========================
>>

>> madness, let me just say we have no plan to actually implement cut()
>> in Stan!

It is interesting that in his MCMCski slides, Martyn basically said the only way to get this to work currently would be via "multiple imputation", basically passing a draw from the PK posterior distribution as "fixed" data for the PD posterior distribution. It seems to me that if we were capable of continuing a Markov Chain and could change the data, possibly with a limited re-adaptation as opposed to a full adaptation from scratch, then people would be able to do what they want (whether that is a good idea or not) with the PK-PD models. And since we have other reasons why continuing a Markov Chain and / or changing the data would be useful, we should just prioritize that a little bit more. In the meantime, people could estimate both models and do some matching thing.

Ben

If you're wrapping CmdStan, there is now a tag for v2.5.0 based in the v2.5.0 tag of Stan. Example models doesn't have a tag, but the tagged version of CmdStan has a commit hash associated with it.

In the earlier output, it looks like you did "make stan-update" which will update to the latest development branch of Stan within CmdStan. "make stan-revert" will set it back to the commit hash that's associated with the CmdStan commit

I think what you should do is:
cd cmdstan
git checkout v2.5.0
make stan-revert

Or something else to get you to the exact commit for each of the submodules.

messages.subject: Over-Conservative Adaptation
messages.body_plain:
As Ben first brought up a few months ago the step size adaptation seems to be
way too conservative, at least for simple models.  For example, setting he target
average acceptance probability to 0.8 can yield an empirical average of 0.9, and
setting the target to 0.7 can yield an empirical average of 0.8.

This was really annoying for the workshop where all we had were simple models,
so I decided to take a deeper look into what might be going on, and here’s my
best guess.

Recall that the symplectic integrators we use are well-behaved up to some step size
where they diverge.  Let’s call that step size epsilon_bad.  In a complex model the
optimal step size will be way below epsilon_bad, ave_accept_prob(epsilon) will be
roughly symmetric, and the Nesterov dual average works well.

On the other hand, in a simple model the optimal step size can be right up against the
divergence threshold.  In a simple Gaussian, for example, the step size isn’t limited
by the stable error but by the divergence.  This manifests as ave_accept_prob(epsilon)
being highly skewed, with a rapid divergence between the optimal step size and
epsilon_bad.  Consequently the dual average creeps up to the optimal step size
from below until it passes it and starts to diverge.  The divergences induce a correction
that pushes the test value to much smaller values at which point the dual average
begins to creep up again.

optimal value.  The most likely outcome is ending up below the optimal step size (with
too high of an optimal acceptance probability) and increasing the terminal buffer (where
we learn the final step size) doesn’t really do anything because the convergence is
so slow.

quadratic and the convergence of the dual averaging suffers accordingly.  Anyone
have any thoughts?  Should we be satisfied with this behavior or try to generalize
our adaptation to identify this situation and respond accordingly?
